questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical CKAD skills: per-namespace scope, Pod image inspection, external API interaction, and secure data handling with Secrets, ConfigMaps, and PVCs.

## Key Concepts
- Namespace-scoped Deployments and Pods
- InitContainers for bootstrap tasks
- Secrets for API tokens and minimal exposure
- ConfigMaps for status storage
- PVC-based log streaming
- NetworkPolicy to restrict egress
- Probes for reliability and readiness

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: ns-security-baseline
  namespace: <target-namespace>
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: installer
        image: busybox
        command: ["sh","-c","apk add --no-cache curl jq || true"]
      containers:
      - name: baseline-scanner
        image: registry.example/scanner:latest
        env:
        - name: CVE_API_URL
          value: "https://cve-feed.example/api/v1/cves"
        - name: API_TOKEN
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: cve-token
              key: token
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: ns-logs
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you rotate the Secret token without downtime?
- How would you scale the scanner across namespaces while keeping per-namespace isolation?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

This question tests practical RBAC auditing skills within the CKAD scope, including multi-namespace governance, secure logging, and egress constraints.

## Key Concepts

- **RBAC objects**: RoleBindings, ClusterRoleBindings, and ServiceAccounts at the namespace level
- **ConfigMap-driven policy**: External policy reference for audit rules
- **Namespace-scoped auditing**: Decentralized audit model vs. cluster-wide approaches
- **Pod lifecycle**: InitContainers for tool installation, readiness/liveness probes for reliability
- **Storage**: PVC-backed logging at /logs
- **Network security**: Namespace NetworkPolicy restricting egress to the audit endpoint

## Trade-offs

- **Pros**: Decentralized scaling, namespace isolation, ConfigMap flexibility for policy updates
- **Cons**: Resource overhead per namespace, potential for policy drift, Secret management complexity, duplicated effort across namespaces

## Minimal YAML Skeleton

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: rbac-policy
data:
  policy.yaml: |-
    allowedBindings:
      - kind: User
        name: admin
    maxServiceAccounts: 10
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: audit-credentials
type: Opaque
stringData:
  bearer-token: <token>
  endpoint: https://audit.example.com/api/v1/digest
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: audit-logs
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: rbac-auditor
  namespace: target-ns
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: rbac-auditor
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: rbac-auditor
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: install-tools
          image: busybox
          command:
            - sh
            - -c
            - "wget -qO /tools/curl https://curl.se/download && wget -qO /tools/jq https://github.com/jqlang/jq/releases/download/jq-1.7.1/jq-linux64 && chmod +x /tools/*"
          volumeMounts:
            - name: tools
              mountPath: /tools
      containers:
        - name: auditor
          image: alpine:latest
          command:
            - sh
            - -c
            - |
              apk add --no-cache curl jq
              while true; do
                kubectl get rolebindings,clusterrolebindings,serviceaccounts -o json > /logs/snapshot.json
                curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -d @/logs/snapshot.json $ENDPOINT
                sleep 3600
              done
          env:
            - name: TOKEN
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: audit-credentials
                  key: bearer-token
            - name: ENDPOINT
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: audit-credentials
                  key: endpoint
          volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 15
            periodSeconds: 20
      volumes:
        - name: logs
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: audit-logs
        - name: tools
          emptyDir: {}
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: audit-egress-restrict
  namespace: target-ns
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: rbac-auditor
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: audit-api
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 443
```

## Why This Is Asked

- Deployment, ConfigMap, resources, probes, HPA

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical CKAD skills: secure container runtime, init containers, config-driven rollouts, resource limits, probes, graceful termination, disruption budgets, and network isolation.

## Key Concepts
- SecurityContext and podSecurityContext for non-root operation
- InitContainer usage and seed data from ConfigMap
- Rolling restart triggers via checksum/config annotation
- Probes and termination settings
- PodDisruptionBudget and NetworkPolicy integration

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal patch skeleton (conceptual)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: worker
spec:
  replicas: 2
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        checksum/config: "<computed-from-configmap>"
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
      containers:
        - name: worker
          image: myorg/worker:latest
          securityContext:
            runAsUser: 1000
            runAsGroup: 1000
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            capabilities:
              drop: ["ALL"]
          env: []
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /data
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "100m"
              memory: "128Mi"
            limits:
              cpu: "500m"
              memory: "256Mi"
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 8080
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: 8080
      initContainers:
        - name: seed-data
          image: busybox
          command: ["sh", "-c", "cp /config/bootstrap/* /data/" ]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /data
            - name: config
              mountPath: /config
      volumes:
        - name: data
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: worker-data-pvc
        - name: config
          configMap:
            name: worker-config
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you automate the checksum calculation for the config annotation in CI/CD?
- How would you verify rollback behavior in a live cluster without affecting production traffic?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests knowledge of VolumeSnapshot APIs, per-namespace scheduling, and how to surface status and logs from a snapshot operation while enforcing network boundaries.

## Key Concepts
- VolumeSnapshot and VolumeSnapshotClass
- Per-namespace CronJob scope
- ConfigMap as status store
- Logs via PVC mounted at /logs
- InitContainer for tooling installation
- Pod readiness/liveness probes
- Namespace NetworkPolicy for egress control

## Code Example
```yaml
# CronJob skeleton
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: snapshot-app-data
  namespace: <ns>
spec:
  schedule: "0,30 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          initContainers:
          - name: init-tools
            image: alpine:3.18
            command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl kubectl; sleep 0"]
          containers:
          - name: snapshotter
            image: my-snapshot-agent:latest
            volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
          volumes:
          - name: logs
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: logs-<ns>
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          nodeSelector:
            kubernetes.io/os: linux
```

```yaml
# VolumeSnapshot skeleton
apiVersion: snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1

metadata:
  name: snap-app-data-<ns>

spec:
  volumeSnapshotClassName: csi-snap
  source:
    persistentVolumeClaimName: app-data
```

## Why This Is Asked
Tests the ability to compose CKAD primitives into a small, observable application with proper security and observability patterns.

## Key Concepts
- ConfigMaps and Secrets for configuration management
- InitContainers and Sidecars for application lifecycle management
- Probes (readiness and liveness) for health monitoring
- Namespace NetworkPolicy for traffic security
- RBAC basics for in-namespace metrics access
- Observability and security trade-offs in containerized applications

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal Deployment sketch
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: python-api
  namespace: target-namespace
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: python-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: python-api
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: install-deps
        image: python:3.11-alpine
        command: ['sh', '-c', 'pip install -r /app/requirements.txt']
        volumeMounts:
        - name: app-code
          mountPath: /app
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: python:3.11-alpine
        command: ['python', '/app/main.py']
        env:
        - name: ENABLE_METRICS
          valueFrom:
            configMapKeyRef:
              name: app-config
              key: ENABLE_METRICS
        - name: API_USERNAME
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: api-credentials
              key: username
        - name: API_PASSWORD
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: api-credentials
              key: password
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
        volumeMounts:
        - name: app-code
          mountPath: /app
      - name: cert-rotator
        image: cert-manager/cert-manager-rotator:latest
        volumeMounts:
        - name: certs
          mountPath: /etc/certs
      volumes:
      - name: app-code
        configMap:
          name: app-code
      - name: certs
        emptyDir: {}
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: restrict-egress
  namespace: target-namespace
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          name: monitoring
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 9000
```

## Trade-offs
- **Security vs. Complexity**: NetworkPolicy adds security but increases deployment complexity
- **Resource Overhead**: Sidecar containers double resource requirements for cert management
- **Observability Cost**: Metrics endpoint requires additional monitoring infrastructure
- **InitContainer Impact**: Dependency installation extends pod startup time
- **Namespace Isolation**: Per-namespace design improves security boundaries but requires duplicate configuration management

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical knowledge of namespace-scoped governance primitives and their impact on scheduling, pod density, and autoscaler behavior.

## Key Concepts
- **ResourceQuota** enforces hard caps on total namespace resource consumption (CPU, memory, pod count, etc.)
- **LimitRange** sets defaults and constraints for individual pod/container resource requests and limits
- Quota enforcement affects scheduler decisions, pod scheduling failures, and autoscaler calculations
- Use `kubectl describe resourcequota <name> --namespace=<ns>` and `kubectl top pod` to monitor usage

## Code Example

```yaml
# Namespace
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: quota-demo
---
# ResourceQuota
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: ns-quota
  namespace: quota-demo
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "4"
    requests.memory: "8Gi"
    limits.cpu: "8"
    limits.memory: "16Gi"
    pods: "20"
---
# LimitRange
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: ns-limits
  namespace: quota-demo
spec:
  limits:
  - type: Container
    default:
      cpu: 500m
      memory: 512Mi
    defaultRequest:
      cpu: 250m
      memory: 256Mi
    max:
      cpu: "2"
      memory: "4Gi"
    min:
      cpu: 100m
      memory: 128Mi
---
# Deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: quota-demo-app
  namespace: quota-demo
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: demo
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: demo
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: nginx
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: 100m
            memory: 128Mi
          limits:
            cpu: 500m
            memory: 512Mi
```

## Trade-offs
- **Flexibility vs. Control**: Quotas prevent resource hoarding but require developers to specify requests/limits, increasing YAML complexity
- **Utilization Risk**: Overly restrictive quotas lead to pod scheduling failures; overly generous quotas waste resources
- **Debugging Overhead**: Quota-induced failures (e.g., "pods quota exceeded") add a layer of complexity to troubleshooting
- **Autoscaler Interaction**: VPA/HPA behavior changes when quotas constrain available headroom

```yaml
kind: Job
metadata:

spec:

      restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to design a maintenance task that runs in Kubernetes using CronJob, PVCs, and ConfigMaps. It also covers secrets, sidecars, probes, and egress constraints in a realistic operational scenario.

## Key Concepts
- Kubernetes CronJob, PersistentVolumeClaim, ConfigMap, Secret
- InitContainer, TLS sidecar, probes, resource requests
- NetworkPolicy, rollback strategy

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: log-cleaner
  namespace: analytics
spec:
  schedule: '0 * * * *'
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: cleaner
            image: registry.example.com/log-cleaner:latest
            volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs/app
            envFrom:
            - configMapRef:
                name: log-retention
          initContainers:
          - name: tools
            image: alpine:3.18
            command: ['sh', '-c', 'apk add --no-cache gzip pigz curl']
          volumes:
          - name: logs
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: logs-pvc
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you verify that log files are pruned and compressed under load?
- How would you rollback a CronJob update and validate it touched no data loss?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical CKAD mastery: per-namespace isolation, InitContainer usage, secret/config management, and production-grade guarantees.

## Key Concepts
- InitContainer for model pull from Secret
- ConfigMap and Secret usage for runtime parameters
- Probes and HPA for reliability and scale
- Idempotent DB writes to achieve at-least-once delivery
- NetworkPolicy to enforce namespace boundaries

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: ns-image-resize
  namespace: <ns>
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: image-resize
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: fetch-model
          image: alpine:3.18
          command: ["sh", "-c", "download-model.sh"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: model
              mountPath: /models
      containers:
        - name: processor
          image: registry/ns-image-resize:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          envFrom:
            - secretRef: { name: resize-secret }
      volumes:
        - name: model
          emptyDir: {}
      readinessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /healthz
          port: 8080
        initialDelaySeconds: 5
        periodSeconds: 10
      livenessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /healthz
          port: 8080
        initialDelaySeconds: 15
        periodSeconds: 20
      affinity:
        podAntiAffinity:
          preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
            - weight: 100
              podAffinityTerm:
                labelSelector:
                  matchLabels:
                    app: image-resize
                topologyKey: "kubernetes.io/hostname"
  ```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you monitor idempotency and retry behavior?
- What changes if Kafka offset management moves to a separate transactional store?

questions.explanation:
Why This Is Asked
- Tests knowledge of per-namespace tooling with standard CKAD primitives (PVCs, InitContainers, ConfigMaps, Secrets, sidecars, probes, NetworkPolicy).
- Exercises end-to-end flow: manifest reading, batching, external POST, and secure networking.

Key Concepts
- InitContainer installation of scanners
- PVC-mounted manifests and ConfigMap-driven batching
- Secret-based credentials and TLS rotation sidecar
- Readiness/Liveness probes and per-namespace NetworkPolicy
- Minimal YAML skeleton and trade-offs between latency and throughput

Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: image-scan-guardian
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: image-scan-guardian
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: image-scan-guardian
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: scanner
          image: alpine:3.18
          command: ["sh", "-c", "while true; do sleep 60; done"]
          volumeMounts:
            - mountPath: /images
              name: images
        - name: main
          image: busybox:1.36
          command: ["sh", "-c", "echo running; sleep 3600"]
          envFrom:
            - configMapRef:
                name: image-config
      initContainers:
        - name: install-scanner
          image: alpine:3.18
          command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache --update curl jq && echo scanner installed"]
      volumes:
        - name: images
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: images-pvc
      imagePullSecrets:
        - name: reg secret
```

Follow-up Questions
- How would you handle partial failures in batch processing?
- What RBAC changes are appropriate for this per-namespace task?
